stops.name: Death at sea, southwest of the Cape Verde Islands
stops.campa: On the twenty-third of June, some days short of any landfall, Pedro de Mendoza dies in his cabin, forty-nine or fifty years old, the disease he carried out of the sack of Rome having finally finished what the famine and the siege and the grief could not. There is no burial ground to receive him: the crew commits his body to the ocean he crossed twice, off the Cape Verde Islands, and the ship carries on to Spain without its adelantado, bearing only his testament and the news of a colony he will never learn was, within four years, already dying behind him.

stops.name: Asunción founded: the frontier moves north
stops.campa: On the feast of the Assumption, Juan de Salazar de Espinosa, acting under the authority Mendoza left to Ayolas, raises a fort on a high bank of the Paraguay river and names it Nuestra Señora de la Asunción. The dying adelantado's enterprise, aimed at a coast, has already begun its long migration inland and north, toward Guaraní allies, toward the rumor of the sierra de la plata, away from the starving fort on the Riachuelo that gave the whole river its name and cannot, for now, keep a single Spaniard alive upon its bank.

stops.name: Buenos Aires burned and abandoned: Irala's order
stops.campa: Four years after Mendoza sailed, Domingo Martínez de Irala, governing now from Asunción, orders the last handful of settlers still clinging to the ruined coastal fort to abandon it and come north; toward the end of June the settlers burn the beached hulk that had served as their fortress, the church, and the timber houses, and march away. Ruy Díaz de Guzmán will later record what is left behind on the empty plain: five mares and seven horses, too few and too wild to be worth driving inland, given over to the grass with no one left to claim them.

stops.name: The wild herds multiply; the plain begins to thunder
stops.campa: In less than a generation, Guzmán's chronicle marvels, the five mares and seven horses left behind at Buen Ayre have multiplied past counting: herds like moving hills range from Cabo Blanco to the fort at Gaboto, eighty leagues and more, and inland to the first rise of the sierras. No wolf, no lion, no herdsman checks them; the pampa that could not feed two thousand Spaniards feeds, untended, tens of thousands of horses gone back to the grass their Andalusian great-grandsires never grazed. The canon of the pampas, the cimarrón, the baqueano, the gaucho still to come, begins here, in an abandonment nobody meant as a gift.

stops.name: Garay's second founding, the plain thundering with horses
stops.campa: Forty-four years after Mendoza's first fort, Juan de Garay comes down from Asunción with sixty families, Guaraní allies, and cattle, and founds Buenos Aires a second time, laying out two hundred and fifty blocks around a fort and a plaza on nearly the same shore. Garay writes home in frustration that the land is so flat and open his men cannot corral a single one of the wild horses running loose upon it; among the Guaraní who ride with him, one cacique called Bagual gallops off free into the open pampa, and gives to every unbroken horse of the country to come his own name.
stops.quote: Until now, because the land is so flat and open, we have not been able to capture any of the horses, nor have we had the possibility and the space to make corrals...
stops.quote_source: Letter of Juan de Garay, cited in historical accounts of the 1580 second founding of Buenos Aires

stops.name: Hernandarias and the mozos perdidos
stops.campa: Hernando Arias de Saavedra, criollo governor of Río de la Plata and Paraguay, writes in frustration of a population he cannot tax, conscript, or hold: the mozos perdidos, the lost boys of the plain between the Paraná, the Uruguay and the Negro, criollo second sons, escaped slaves, freed prisoners, abandoned youth, all gone native on the grass and the freed herds Mendoza's abandonment first set loose. They ride the cimarrón horses no one owns, eat the cimarrón cattle no one branded, and answer to no crown; the word gaucho does not yet exist to name them, but the thing it will name already rides the pampa Hernandarias cannot govern.

stops.name: The ombú, the gaucho's horse, and Martín Fierro
stops.campa: Across the treeless pampa the ombú stands as the only vertical thing on the horizon, the Lighthouse the gauchos call it, its dense canopy the sole shade for the feral children of the plain, human, equine, bovine alike, descended in spirit if not in blood from the horses Mendoza's abandonment first freed. When José Hernández gives the gaucho his epic voice in 1872, the freedom the poem sings is the same freedom the pampa has been offering, and withholding, since 1541: no nest, no master, no one to follow when the bird, or the horse, or the mozo perdido, takes flight.
stops.quote: My glory is to live as free as the bird in the sky; I don't make a nest on this ground, and there is so much to suffer, and no one will follow me when I take flight.
stops.quote_source: José Hernández, El gaucho Martín Fierro (1872)

stops.name: Parque Lezama, the monument at the departure
stops.campa: Four hundred years to the day after Mendoza died at sea, the Academia Nacional de la Historia's judgment that this bluff above the old Riachuelo shore was his true site raises, in the same Parque Lezama, a stone monument to the sick adelantado who abandoned this ground and, in abandoning it, set loose the herd that outlived his colony by centuries. The same city will grow, on this ground, the atlas's own densest cluster of departures and returns: Belgrano's flag, Alvear's exile, Evita's body, Charly's piano, every one of them descended, in the end, from the horses no one meant to set free.
